title: Avoiding streetcars, buses and the colour line
summary: Streetcar segregation memories, his wife's hardships for being light-skinned, and tiredness at 64.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: How long has it been since you've been on a streetcar?
Oh, my goodness. It has to be 60-some years.
And do you ever ride the buses today?
Never do. I don't ride the buses in San Antonio. I don't ride the buses here.
Do you really feel that you don't like the high day of the bus?

Maybe it was a disappointment in my young days when I used to have to get on the streetcar and take and move the screen back for me to get a seat. I've always been conscious of being what they call a Negro. And you're brought up to know that this is your place here and this is your place there. You don't go here and you don't go there. And as I got older and I started fighting for civil rights and things like that, then there's some things that irritate you that you don't want to be reminded of. So I stay away from places like the buses and the streetcars.
And Dutch, you tell me she had?

Oh, Dutch, she caught holy hell in her days because she's so light and she had yellow hair. But the Negroes didn't want to accept her. When the white people found out she was a Negro, they didn't want to accept her. So it's been a problem.

Well, you know, I saw her yesterday and it takes you aback when you see her. You know, it's hard for me to realize it looking at it from the standpoint of being white, that she's not white, you know, when you first see her.
Right. Well, that's been the problem she's had.
Oh, we've suffered quite a lot.
But you can't give up your fight for something you believe in.

You don't. You don't give up. The only thing you give up, you have to give up to your age. See, when I was young, I could fight and fight and fight. But Ma, at 64 years old, man, the fight's almost gone.
